The caption that goes with this photograph in our archives reads:
"Walk Match at Battersea circa 1938. Starters include H.G. Churcher, C.E.Churcher, D.E. Brown, A.A.Harley, F. Jarvis, C.W.Redgrave."
Our first stab at actually naming the faces came up with Don Brown (1), Harry Churcher (7), Charlie Churcher (23), C.W. Redgrave (24) and Alf Harley (behind Brown). However, as others have become involved and have cast their eyes over the picture, we are now not at all sure of anyone except Alf Harley. For instance, we are told that Charlie Churcher did not wear glasses and the chap next to Harry, second from the left, may be Jack Rutland If any reader can help us with more specific details of the race then we would be very pleased to hear from them.

* Edward Heath has his music - Alfred Harley has his amateur dramatics - here he is seen in, "Lockhart's Last Case" with a strong supporting cast. In the background it looks like Charlie MacLennan (without trousers) taking finger-prints and the immediate foreground are three heads waiting for the chop whilst the amiable assistant "Tinker" is being carpeted by the boss.

photos.c: It's the Club Championship 880 yds of 1946 and the setting is Tooting Bec track. Just look at those crowds; over half the track was lined like that. Taking the lead, which he held to the end, is Len Marchant who won in 1:59.0 from Len Herbert (4th from right) and Jack Brown (6th from right).

Len Herbert and Bill Lucas were often involved in battle royal. Len, who gained his international vest in 1946, invariably used to sit in on the taller, longer striding Bill, waiting to turn on his powerful sprint in the final stretch. But on this occasion, believed to be at Wimbledon Stadium in 1951, Bill held the sprinter at bay. W.E. "Bill "Lucas, DFC, made his international debut in the heats of the 1948 Olympic 5,000m.

Left: Nearly two miles gone in the '5¾'. It's September 1966 and among the 39 competitors in the race, this bunch are out to settle personal scores - or perhaps just enjoy the sunshine. The runners are: Financial wizards Keith Miller (106) and Jim Heathfield (93), Ted Pallant (94), talented youth and junior Tony Brooks (37) - lost to the sport before making impact as a senior, Dave McMillan (12) - now fighting back from terrible injuries sustained while out training and hit by a car, P.Blair-Fish (46).

Above: Chas (18) tears into the lead on the first lap of a Club Championship 880 yards Race at Battersea Park. We are not absolutely certain of the year but it was probably 1955, one of the years when Charlie Walker, (4) at the back of the pack became Club Champion over the distance. Behind Charlie Manning can be seen a youthful Jim Heathfield. Can anyone put names to the other faces in the picture?

Above: The 70s and a photo call after a Young Athletes Sunday morning training session at Wimbledon Park. The adults, left of the group, left to right are: John Martin, Frank Simmons, Jim Heathfield (crouching), Bob Taylor, Reg. Hopkins Jnr., Reg Hopkins Snr. Below: There's a fair few miles been walked by the legs belonging to these two gents. For Eric Hall (left) it was fifty years since his first turn-out in a Belgrave '7'. He placed 140th that day in 1948 (31st Belgravian home with another two behind him) in a race won by Harry Churcher. George Beecham (right) will be celebrating the half a century since his début in this race in 2000.

Happy with a seventh successive year in the medals at the National Road Relay. Top left. Kevin Clarke (83) demonstrates the cross leg shuffle as he takes the baton from new member L.Lyons.

photos.c: Above: Top left to right - Ollie Foote, second Belgravian home at Coulsdon, a hirsute Frank Ward (we hear he has taken it off for his wedding) and Marco Mazzotta., who has steadily improved since last Autumn. Bottom - Jon Hobbs, Andy Paton and Don Anderson, the man who runs the Club '10' and then goes round again to collect the flags (and probably went round before to set them up!

Opposite page: The "last" Belgrave-Southern Relay.
Top. High noon and the starter sends 61 runners off on the first leg. Jon Hobbs completes his lap of the "top" and nears the crowd at the Hand in Hand.
Centre. Ollie Foote sends Marcello Bizio away on the last stage. Jim Estall loosens up for the London Marathon with a 25:53 long leg. Second fastest long stage of the day and another mark in the all-time top 20 - Paul Evans has an easy run!
Bottom. Jim Estall launches Marco Mazzotta. Frank Ward reaches the summit of Wool Road. Putting on a good show for visiting relations, "Aussie" Brandon Reid streaks off the Common for a nippy second leg.

photos.c: Wearing the English Rose, M40 Jim Estall (220) grafts away at the head of the Home Countries International Veterans' Cross Country Champs. at Ballymena on November 8th.  It's the fourth of  five laps and still no-one has been able to dominate the field.  However, the tattooed Rob Wise, close up behind Jim at this point, was soon to make a decisive move.  Gerry Brady (211) of Ireland was unable to respond while Mike Hagar and Jim gave chase.  On the final lap the Belgravian overtook Hagar to gain a clear 2nd in 31:55 but Wise at 31:37 was out of reach.

photos.c: Rob Harding, Ray Foley, Mike Webb, Clive Gilby, Kevin Quinn, Jim Estall John Mather and Lee Hurst steel themselves for the start of the first Surrey League race of 1998-99.

1. One of the most glorious sights in athletics is the start of the Senior Men's National Cross Country Championships. Half a mile into the 2000 race at Stowe School, Buckinghhamshire, and the field is led by Belgrave's Paul Evans with Paul Freary just behind him and to the right. On the left, behind 2516 is Kevin Nash and next but one above 2321 is Rob McHarg. On the right, behind the orange vested .24 is Jason Lobo, making a more conservative start, with Lee Hurst next but one on the left of .24. In the centre, just behind and to the right of the Blackheath vest is Alaster Stewart and next on the right, with only his claret bandana showing is Charles Herrington. That's eight in the top 100 and they spent the next half mile gaining even more forward positions. You might have to take the Editor's word for this one: on the skyline just to the left of the tree can be seen Phil Carstairs' thinning thatch. Will Cockerell has also been picked out in this vicinity by one viewer - but blowed if we can find him now!
Fastest 'A' team man at the Southern 6-Stage - Lee Hurst
Below: Ignoring the pouring rain at the end of the race. Lee Hurst, Paul Freary, Spencer Barden, Jason Lobo, Paul Evans and Mark Miles.

Right: An hour before "National" race time. Bill Laws and John Jeffery have driven back to Milton Keynes to pick up Paul Evans whose car has broken down, leaving the rest of the team to pose for the pre-race photo. Back row: Eric Hall (President), Don Anderson, Paul Coughlan, Alan Mead, Alaster Stewart, Paul Freary, Jason Lobo, Kevin Nash, Phil Carstairs, Rob Harding. Front: Darryl Ochse, Will Cockerell, Charles Herrington, Lee Hurst, Rob McHarg.
Below: Twice he's run and twice he's won. Lee Hurst receives the the "Parker Bowl," reserved for the first Belgrave man home in the National, from President Eric Hall.

Belgrave's Winning AAA 12-Stage Team at Sutton Park. Back row: Andy Graffin, Spencer Barden, Paul Freary, Stephen Sharp, Alaster Stewart, David Anderson, Allen Graffin, Paul Evans. Front row: Lee Hurst, Mark Miles, Alan Mead (team manager), Richard Ward, Charles Herrington.

mentions.note: pictured finishing the Surrey Road Relay Championship, 9 September 1961, his last race, taking South London Harriers to victory
three consecutive National cross-country titles; world records at 3000m (twice), 5000m and 6 miles; won 1953 Emsley Carr Mile; died aged 61

photos.c:
The last stride in the last race of an illustrious career. Gordon Pirie crosses the line in the Surrey Road Relay Championship of 9th September 1961, taking South London Harriers to victory. Gordon's time was a full two minutes faster than any one else on that day.
Three weeks later "The People" ran a series of articles in which Pirie confessed to being paid to run, revealed that some of his opponents had resorted to drugs, and generally blew the lid off the cosy world of "amateur" athletics.

Photo from the collection owned by Clive Shippen.
Right: The photo on the cover of Dick Booth's book shows Gordon Pirie winning the AAA 3 miles Championship at White City, Shepherd's Bush, London on July 11th 1953.
